etymology: From the Latin pelicanus, from the Greek pelekan, a large water-fowl with a pouched bill; rendering the Hebrew qa'ath, a bird of the waste places named among the unclean fowls.
biblical_def: The pelican is a great pouch-billed water-fowl, listed among the fowls Israel might not eat: “And the swan, and the pelican, and the gier eagle” (Lev 11:18; cf. Deu 14:17). But the word is remembered chiefly for one line of a broken man’s prayer. The psalmist, in the psalm titled a prayer of the afflicted when he is overwhelmed, cries, “I am like a pelican of the wilderness: I am like an owl of the desert” (Psa 102:6), and adds, “I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top” (Psa 102:7). He does not mean he is unclean; he means he is alone. The pelican is a bird of water, and he is in a waste place; the pelican is a bird of the flock, and he sits solitary. That is the whole picture of affliction — a creature out of its element, cut off from its kind, crying where no ear seems to hear. And the psalm does not leave him there. Against his own withering it sets an unwithering God: “But thou, O LORD, shalt endure for ever; and thy remembrance unto all generations” (Psa 102:12), and then the promise the destitute live on, that “he will regard the prayer of the destitute, and not despise their prayer” (Psa 102:17). The pelican of the wilderness is heard.
webster_summary: A large water-fowl with a pouched bill; named among the unclean fowls, and the emblem of the solitary sufferer.
webster_full: PELICAN, a large fowl of the water, having a great bag or pouch beneath the bill.
From the Latin pelicanus, from the Greek pelekan.
Numbered with the fowls forbidden to Israel for meat (Lev 11:18).
Used by the psalmist as a figure of desolate solitude (Psa 102:6).
A bird of the waters found in a waste place — a creature out of its element.
scriptures: And the swan, and the pelican, and the gier eagle,
And the pelican, and the gier eagle, and the cormorant,
I am like a pelican of the wilderness: I am like an owl of the desert.
But thou, O LORD, shalt endure for ever; and thy remembrance unto all generations.
corruption_summary: The old emblem of the solitary sufferer, now re-labelled as a condition to be medicated rather than a cry to be carried to God.
corruption_paragraphs: The live misuse is the reduction of the psalmist’s cry to a diagnosis. Our age hears “I am like a pelican of the wilderness” and reaches immediately for a clinical label, as though the whole account of the man were a chemistry to be corrected and not a soul to be comforted. Scripture is not against the physician, and the body’s frailty is real; but the psalm treats the affliction as something to be prayed, not merely managed. The title of the psalm says it plainly: a prayer of the afflicted, when he is overwhelmed, and poureth out his complaint before the LORD. The complaint is poured before the LORD. Where that direction is lost, a man may be soothed and still be alone, treated and still unheard.

The remedy the psalm supplies is not a better feeling but a greater God. The sufferer measures his days as a shadow that declineth and his own withering as grass, and then turns the corner on one word: but thou. “But thou, O LORD, shalt endure for ever.” The pelican’s wilderness is real and the pelican’s God is unchanged, and the second fact outlives the first. It is precisely to the destitute — the emptied, the stripped, the man with no case to plead — that the promise is made that their prayer will not be despised. The bird in the waste place is not forgotten by the One who put it there, and the affliction that drives a man to solitude is the very thing appointed to drive him to prayer.
roots_summary: A great water-fowl of the pouched bill, unclean under the law and the emblem of the desolate.
roots_lines: Pelican — Latin pelicanus, Greek pelekan; Hebrew qa'ath.
Listed among the unclean fowls of Lev 11:18 and Deu 14:17.
A water-bird, so a pelican in the wilderness is a creature out of its element.
Psa 102:6 makes it the figure of the overwhelmed and solitary soul.
The psalm answers the figure with the LORD who endureth for ever (Psa 102:12).
usage: A pelican of the wilderness: a water-bird in a waste place, and a soul out of its element.
The psalmist does not say he is unclean; he says he is alone.
Set the pelican’s wilderness beside the but thou of Psa 102:12, and the wilderness is outlived.

etymology: From the Middle English bitoure, through the Old French butor, a marsh-bird of the heron kind known for its deep booming cry; rendering the Hebrew qippod, a creature of ruined and waterlogged places.
biblical_def: The bittern is a solitary marsh-fowl, a bird of reeds and standing water, whose booming call carries over an empty fen. Scripture never sets it in a pleasant landscape. It appears where a proud city has been unmade. Against Babylon the LORD swears, “I will also make it a possession for the bittern, and pools of water: and I will sweep it with the besom of destruction, saith the LORD of hosts” (Isa 14:23). The palaces are not merely emptied; the ground itself reverts to swamp, and a wading bird takes the freehold of the place that ruled the nations. So also over Idumea: “But the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also and the raven shall dwell in it: and he shall stretch out upon it the line of confusion, and the stones of emptiness” (Isa 34:11). Zephaniah puts the same bird in Nineveh’s ruined doorways: “both the cormorant and the bittern shall lodge in the upper lintels of it; their voice shall sing in the windows; desolation shall be in the thresholds” (Zep 2:14). The doctrine is the sovereignty of God over empires. He does not merely defeat a city; He reassigns its title-deed to the birds. What Babylon called eternal, the LORD hands over to a heron, and the last sound in the throne-room is a bittern’s cry in the reeds.
webster_summary: A marsh-fowl of the heron kind, of deep booming cry; in Scripture the tenant of cities God has laid waste.
webster_full: BITTERN, a fowl of the grallic order and heron kind, frequenting fens and marshy places.
From Middle English bitoure, Old French butor; Hebrew qippod.
Noted for the hollow booming note it utters among the reeds.
Babylon is made a possession for the bittern and pools of water (Isa 14:23).
It lodges with the cormorant in Nineveh’s upper lintels (Zep 2:14).
scriptures: I will also make it a possession for the bittern, and pools of water: and I will sweep it with the besom of destruction, saith the LORD of hosts.
But the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also and the raven shall dwell in it: and he shall stretch out upon it the line of confusion, and the stones of emptiness.
Zep 2:14

And flocks shall lie down in the midst of her, all the beasts of the nations: both the cormorant and the bittern shall lodge in the upper lintels of it; their voice shall sing in the windows; desolation shall be in the thresholds: for he shall uncover the cedar work.
Rev 18:2

And he cried mightily with a strong voice, saying, Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit, and a cage of every unclean and hateful bird.
corruption_summary: The desolation oracles are read today as poetic exaggeration; Scripture presents them as sworn judgments that history executed.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the treatment of these oracles as literary flourish — grand language about the fall of empires, not a word from the LORD of hosts about particular cities on particular ground. But Isa 14:23 is not a poet’s hyperbole; it is a divine oath, sealed saith the LORD of hosts, and it names the instrument (the besom of destruction), the outcome (pools of water), and the tenant (the bittern). Babylon fell. Nineveh fell. The mounds and marshes are where the prophets said they would be. Prophecy that specific is either the word of God or a fraud, and the ruins have already voted. To file the desolation oracles under imagery is to blunt the only thing they were given to do, which is to make proud men afraid of God in time.

The doctrine to recover is that the LORD disposes of nations as He pleases and leaves a bird as the receipt. Babylon boasted herself a lady for ever; the LORD deeded her to a marsh-fowl. Nineveh sat carelessly and said, I am, and there is none beside me; her lintels became a perch. And John, seeing the last Babylon fall, uses the same image sharpened — “a cage of every unclean and hateful bird” (Rev 18:2). Every empire that has set itself against Christ is on the same schedule. That is not a threat to the church but her comfort: the kingdoms that terrify her in one century are birdcages in the next, and only the kingdom that cannot be moved remains.
roots_summary: A booming marsh-bird of the heron kind; the appointed tenant of cities under the curse.
roots_lines: Bittern — Middle English bitoure, Old French butor; Hebrew qippod.
A fen-bird whose hollow cry carries across standing water.
Babylon becomes its possession, with pools of water (Isa 14:23).
It possesses Idumea with the cormorant, owl, and raven (Isa 34:11).
It lodges in Nineveh’s lintels where princes once stood (Zep 2:14).
usage: A possession for the bittern: the LORD deeds a fallen empire to a marsh-bird.
Where the bittern cries, the line of confusion has been stretched out.
Babylon called herself eternal; the bittern holds the title now.

etymology: From the Old French cormaran, from the Latin corvus marinus, “sea-raven”; a large diving sea-fowl of proverbial greediness, rendering Hebrew names of birds that haunt water and ruins.
biblical_def: The cormorant is a great diving sea-fowl, black and long-necked, so given to swallowing fish that its name became a byword for greed. The law forbids it to Israel’s table: “And the little owl, and the cormorant, and the great owl” (Lev 11:17), and again, “And the pelican, and the gier eagle, and the cormorant” (Deu 14:17). Two things mark nearly every fowl on that list — they live by taking life, and they haunt places of death and waste. The cormorant is both a hunter and a squatter in ruins: “But the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it” (Isa 34:11); “both the cormorant and the bittern shall lodge in the upper lintels of it” (Zep 2:14). The point of the prohibition was never dietetics. It was a daily, edible lesson in separation. Three times a day Israel handled the difference between what God had marked off and what He had not, and the reason given is never hygiene but holiness: “Ye shall therefore put difference between clean beasts and unclean… And ye shall be holy unto me: for I the LORD am holy, and have severed you from other people, that ye should be mine” (Lev 20:25–26). The bird was a schoolmaster. It taught a nation that the line between clean and unclean is drawn by God, and that a severed people eats differently because it belongs differently.
webster_summary: A large voracious sea-fowl of the diving kind; forbidden as food to Israel and a tenant of ruined cities.
webster_full: CORMORANT, a large web-footed fowl of the pelican kind, remarkable for its voracity.
From Old French cormaran, Latin corvus marinus, “sea-raven.”
Figuratively, a glutton; one insatiable in appetite.
Reckoned among the unclean fowls (Lev 11:17; Deu 14:17).
Named with the bittern as possessor of desolated places (Isa 34:11).
scriptures: And the little owl, and the cormorant, and the great owl,
And the pelican, and the gier eagle, and the cormorant,
But the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also and the raven shall dwell in it: and he shall stretch out upon it the line of confusion, and the stones of emptiness.
And ye shall be holy unto me: for I the LORD am holy, and have severed you from other people, that ye should be mine.
corruption_summary: The clean-and-unclean law is dismissed as primitive food superstition; Scripture gives it as the daily catechism of a severed people.
corruption_paragraphs: The common corruption is to explain the unclean-bird list away as ancient sanitation — a pre-modern people fumbling toward food safety and calling it religion. Scripture never gives that reason. The reason it gives is the character of God and the status of His people: I the LORD am holy, and have severed you from other people, that ye should be mine. Reduce the law to hygiene and you have explained the letter while destroying the point. The prohibition was not medicine; it was a boundary marker worn at every meal, so that a nation could not eat a mouthful without remembering that it had been marked off for God and could not live like the nations around it.

The fulfilment is not the abolition of the principle but the arrival of the substance. Christ, declaring the heart to be the seat of defilement, purged all meats (Mar 7:19); Peter on the housetop was told, “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” (Act 10:15); and Paul writes that “every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:4). The dividing wall between Jew and Gentile is down, and the cormorant is not the church’s problem. But the separation the bird taught did not die with the bird — it changed its object. The old line ran between kinds of meat; the new line runs between the world and the holy, and it is drawn just as sharply: “come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing” (2Co 6:17).
roots_summary: The sea-raven — a voracious diving fowl, unclean under the law, tenant of ruins in the oracles.
roots_lines: Cormorant — Old French cormaran, Latin corvus marinus, “sea-raven.”
Its proverbial greed made the name a byword for the glutton.
Forbidden to Israel among the unclean fowls (Lev 11:17; Deu 14:17).
It possesses Idumea and lodges in Nineveh’s lintels (Isa 34:11; Zep 2:14).
The prohibition taught separation, not sanitation (Lev 20:25–26).
usage: The cormorant was forbidden not because it was unwholesome but because Israel was severed.
A cormorant in the lintels is the sign that a city has been handed over.
The clean-and-unclean table was a catechism a nation ate three times a day.

etymology: From the Old English hleapewince, “leap-winker,” from the bird’s tumbling, flickering flight; rendering the Hebrew dukiphath, a crested bird named next to last in the list of unclean fowls.
biblical_def: The lapwing is a small crested bird of erratic, tumbling flight, named near the end of the forbidden fowls: “The stork, the heron after her kind, and the lapwing, and the bat” (Lev 11:19; cf. Deu 14:18). Its chief lesson lies in its position on the list. The law does not stop with the eagle and the vulture, the great and the obvious; it walks all the way down to a crested bird that few would think worth naming and a bat that is not a bird at all. Nothing is left to the Israelite’s judgment. The line between clean and unclean is drawn by God to the last feather, and the closing statement of the chapter says exactly that its purpose is “to make a difference between the unclean and the clean, and between the beast that may be eaten and the beast that may not be eaten” (Lev 11:47). Which modern bird the Hebrew dukiphath names is not certain to us; the hoopoe is the usual identification. That uncertainty is a limit of our knowledge of ancient fauna, not a flaw in the text. Moses wrote a name his hearers recognised at once, and they obeyed without a footnote. What God has spoken remains exact whether or not we can supply the modern label, and the lapwing stands in the list as proof that His law reaches the small things.
webster_summary: A small crested bird of tumbling flight, named among the unclean fowls of the law.
webster_full: LAPWING, a bird of the genus Tringa, having a crest and a flickering, tumbling flight.
From Old English hleapewince, “leap-winker,” from its manner of flying.
Rendering the Hebrew dukiphath, commonly identified with the hoopoe.
Named with the stork, the heron, and the bat as unclean (Lev 11:19).
Repeated in the parallel list at Deu 14:18.
scriptures: The stork, the heron after her kind, and the lapwing, and the bat.
And the stork, and the heron after her kind, and the lapwing, and the bat.
To make a difference between the unclean and the clean, and between the beast that may be eaten and the beast that may not be eaten.
And the voice spake unto him again the second time, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.
corruption_summary: Where a Hebrew creature-name cannot be matched to a modern species, the text is charged with error; the fault is in our zoology, not in the Word.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the habit of treating every gap in our own knowledge as a defect in Scripture. Because the exact bird behind dukiphath cannot be pinned with certainty three thousand years later, the list is presented as vague or confused. It was not vague to Moses and it was not vague to the Israelite who obeyed it. A name that a whole nation used without hesitation has simply passed out of common speech, as English names for creatures pass out of use in a few generations. The inspired text says exactly what God intended it to say; the uncertainty lies in our lexicons of ancient fauna. Verbal plenary inspiration is a claim about what the Word is, not a promise that every ancient bird will keep its passport.

The doctrine to hold is that the law’s reach to the smallest creature was the shadow, and the substance is Christ. The list runs down to the lapwing and the bat because holiness is not a matter of broad strokes but of a line God draws and man does not move. That whole ordinance stood “until the time of reformation” (Heb 9:10), and when the time came the Lord Himself lifted it: “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” (Act 10:15). Peter learned on that housetop that the sheet was never chiefly about birds. It was about the Gentiles — and the God who once numbered every unclean fowl to keep a nation separate now cleanses the nations themselves and gathers them in.
roots_summary: A crested bird of tumbling flight; the small name near the end of the unclean list.
roots_lines: Lapwing — Old English hleapewince, “leap-winker.”
Renders the Hebrew dukiphath, usually identified with the hoopoe.
Listed with the stork, heron, and bat (Lev 11:19; Deu 14:18).
Its place near the end shows the law reaching to the least creature.
The stated purpose is to make a difference between clean and unclean (Lev 11:47).
usage: The law does not stop at the eagle; it walks down to the lapwing and the bat.
That we cannot name the lapwing’s species is a gap in our zoology, not in the text.
A crested bird few would notice is named, because God draws the line and man does not move it.

etymology: The Authorized Version’s spelling of osprey, from the Old French ospres and ultimately the Latin ossifraga, “bone-breaker”; a great fish-hawk, rendering the Hebrew 'ozniyyah.
biblical_def: The ospray is a great fish-hawk, a bird of hooked beak and grappling talons that drops upon its prey out of the air. It stands third in the roll of forbidden fowls, in the company of the largest raptors: “the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray” (Lev 11:13; cf. Deu 14:12). The chapter opens that list with a word heavier than dislike — “these are they which ye shall have in abomination among the fowls” — and the birds that head it share one trait: they live by seizing life and by feeding on blood. That is the key to the whole category. Israel was a people forbidden the blood, for the life of the flesh is in the blood and God had given it upon the altar to make atonement; and a bird that ate blood as its daily bread could never come to the table of a people whose whole religion turned on blood reserved to God. The law was a shadow, “but the body is of Christ” (Col 2:17). The prohibition was not squeamishness about hawks. It was a standing sermon that life belongs to God, that blood is not common, and that the only blood which may be taken and lived upon is the blood God Himself appointed — the blood of His Son, given for many for the remission of sins.
webster_summary: A great fish-hawk of hooked beak and talons; third in the roll of fowls held in abomination.
webster_full: OSPRAY, the sea-eagle or fish-hawk, a large bird of prey that feeds upon fish.
From Old French ospres, from Latin ossifraga, “bone-breaker.”
It seizes its prey by dropping upon it from a height with the talons.
Named with the eagle and the ossifrage as an abomination (Lev 11:13).
Repeated in Moses’ second recital of the law (Deu 14:12).
scriptures: And these are they which ye shall have in abomination among the fowls; they shall not be eaten, they are an abomination: the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray,
But these are they of which ye shall not eat: the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray,

Ye shall therefore put difference between clean beasts and unclean, and between unclean fowls and clean: and ye shall not make your souls abominable by beast, or by fowl, or by any manner of living thing that creepeth on the ground, which I have separated from you as unclean.
Col 2:17
Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.
corruption_summary: The birds of prey are moralised into emblems of cruelty; the law makes them a lesson about blood, and the lesson terminates on the cross.
corruption_paragraphs: The easy misreading is to preach the ospray as a picture of the rapacious man — predatory, grasping, a warning against greed. That is a sermon the text does not give. The bird is not blamed for being what God made it; the eagle’s talons and the hawk’s stoop are the Creator’s handiwork, and the same Lord who forbade the ospray to Israel’s table feeds the young ravens which cry. To moralise the creature is to lose the type. The birds head the abomination list because of what they consume, and what they consume is blood; and blood, in Israel’s whole economy, was the one thing reserved absolutely to God.

The doctrine to recover is that the ceremonial law was not arbitrary and is not obsolete in its meaning, only in its form. Every one of these ordinances was “a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.” The shadow said: life is God’s, blood is holy, no man takes it for himself. The body said: the Son of God poured out His blood, and now the command is not touch it not but drink ye all of it. What was forbidden to the whole nation is commanded to the whole church, because the blood in question is no longer taken by a predator but given by a Redeemer. The ospray on the list and the cup on the table are two ends of one doctrine.
roots_summary: The bone-breaker — a great fish-hawk, third among the fowls held in abomination.
roots_lines: Ospray — the AV spelling of osprey; Latin ossifraga, “bone-breaker.”
Renders the Hebrew 'ozniyyah, a great bird of prey.
Named third in the abomination list, after the eagle and the ossifrage (Lev 11:13).
Birds of prey head the list because they live upon blood.
The prohibition guarded the doctrine that blood belongs to God (Lev 20:25).
usage: The ospray heads the list with the eagle: birds that live by blood.
The bird is not blamed for its talons; the law is teaching Israel about blood.
A shadow of things to come — and the body is of Christ.

etymology: From the Dutch gier, “vulture,” joined to eagle; a vulture-eagle, rendering the Hebrew racham, a carrion-feeding bird named among the unclean fowls.
biblical_def: The gier eagle is a vulture-eagle — the old English joins the Dutch gier, a vulture, to eagle — and it names a carrion-feeder, most commonly identified with the Egyptian vulture. It stands beside the pelican in both lists of forbidden fowls: “And the swan, and the pelican, and the gier eagle” (Lev 11:18); “And the pelican, and the gier eagle, and the cormorant” (Deu 14:17). Where the ospray takes living prey, this bird takes the dead, and that is precisely its disqualification. Under the law, a carcase defiled whatever touched it, and a bird that lived on carcases was itself a walking contradiction of the holiness Israel was called to wear. The reason is given without apology: “And ye shall be holy unto me: for I the LORD am holy, and have severed you from other people, that ye should be mine” (Lev 20:26). Which modern species the Hebrew racham names is not certain to us; the Hebrew names a real bird that every Israelite could point to, and our inability to fix the zoological label is a limit of our knowledge, never a charge against the Word. And the type has found its end. Christ, teaching that defilement comes out of the heart and not into the mouth, purged all meats (Mar 7:19), and Peter was taught the same lesson on a Joppa housetop before he ever set foot in the house of Cornelius.
webster_summary: A vulture-eagle, a feeder on carrion; named among the unclean fowls with the pelican.
webster_full: GIER EAGLE, a vulture of the eagle kind, a feeder upon carrion.
From the Dutch gier, “vulture,” compounded with eagle.
Renders the Hebrew racham, commonly taken as the Egyptian vulture.
Listed with the swan and the pelican as unclean (Lev 11:18; Deu 14:17).
Its diet of carrion is the ground of its exclusion under the law.
scriptures: And the swan, and the pelican, and the gier eagle,
And the pelican, and the gier eagle, and the cormorant,
And ye shall be holy unto me: for I the LORD am holy, and have severed you from other people, that ye should be mine.
Mar 7:19
Because it entereth not into his heart, but into the belly, and goeth out into the draught, purging all meats?
corruption_summary: The old dietary code is treated as a dead letter with nothing to say; in fact it preached separation, and its abolition preached the ingathering of the nations.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is a double one, and the church has fallen into both ditches. The first is the Judaizing instinct that reimposes the shadow — the modern movements that press believers back onto meats and days as though Calvary had left the sheet unclean. Paul settles it: “Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days” (Col 2:16). The second is the opposite error, that the food laws were mere arbitrary taboo with no meaning at all. They had a meaning, stated in the text: I the LORD am holy, and have severed you. A carrion-bird could not come to the table of a severed people because Israel was to be marked in her appetites as in everything else.

The doctrine to recover is the meaning of the abolition. When the Lord purged all meats, He did not merely widen a menu; He announced that the wall between Jew and Gentile was coming down. Peter saw the unclean fowls in a sheet and heard, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common, and then he understood the vision: “God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean” (Act 10:28). The gier eagle on the list and Cornelius at the door are one lesson in two parts. The separation the law taught was never God’s last word about the nations; it was the fence that kept a people distinct until the Seed came in whom all the families of the earth are blessed.
roots_summary: The vulture-eagle — a carrion-feeder excluded from Israel’s table by the law of holiness.
roots_lines: Gier eagle — Dutch gier, “vulture,” + eagle.
Renders the Hebrew racham, usually taken as the Egyptian vulture.
Named with the pelican in both unclean lists (Lev 11:18; Deu 14:17).
It feeds on carrion, and a carcase defiled whatever touched it.
Christ purged all meats, ending the type (Mar 7:19).
usage: The ospray takes the living; the gier eagle takes the dead — both were unclean.
The Hebrew names a real bird; our uncertainty about its species is our limit, not the text’s.
The gier eagle in the sheet and Cornelius at the door are one lesson in two parts.

etymology: From the Old English storc, akin to the German Storch; a great long-legged migratory bird, rendering the Hebrew chasidah, from chesed, kindness — the “kind one,” so named for its care of its young.
biblical_def: The stork is a great white migratory bird, long of leg and neck, nesting high and travelling far. Its Hebrew name chasidah comes from chesed, kindness, for the tenderness it shows toward its young. It is reckoned unclean for the table (Lev 11:19; Deu 14:18), yet its place in Scripture is not chiefly among the abominations but among the witnesses. The fir trees are its house (Psa 104:17), set there by the God who provides for every creature He made. And Jeremiah puts it in the pulpit: “Yea, the stork in the heaven knoweth her appointed times; and the turtle and the crane and the swallow observe the time of their coming; but my people know not the judgment of the LORD” (Jer 8:7). That is the crown text and one of the sharpest rebukes in the prophets. A bird with no law, no covenant, no prophets, and no Scripture keeps the season God appointed for it without fail; a nation with all of these misses the hour of its visitation. The stork obeys by instinct what Judah refused by will. And the indictment goes deeper still, for the very next verse exposes men who said, “We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us” (Jer 8:8), while the pen of the scribes worked in vain. Possession of the Word is not the same as obedience to it. The stork will rise in the judgment against the man who owned a Bible and never kept the season.
webster_summary: A great migratory long-legged bird whose punctual seasons rebuke the disobedience of covenant people.
webster_full: STORK, a large bird of the grallic order, of long legs and bill, migratory in its habits.
From Old English storc; Hebrew chasidah, from chesed, “kindness.”
So named from the care it is observed to take of its young.
Numbered among the unclean fowls (Lev 11:19; Deu 14:18).
The fir trees are her house, and she knows her appointed times (Psa 104:17; Jer 8:7).
scriptures: The stork, the heron after her kind, and the lapwing, and the bat.
Jer 8:7
Yea, the stork in the heaven knoweth her appointed times; and the turtle and the crane and the swallow observe the time of their coming; but my people know not the judgment of the LORD.
Where the birds make their nests: as for the stork, the fir trees are her house.
Jer 8:8
How do ye say, We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us? Lo, certainly in vain made he it; the pen of the scribes is in vain.
corruption_summary: Creation’s witness is treated as sentiment about nature; Jeremiah wields it as a courtroom exhibit against religious men who own the Word and do not keep it.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is a religion of possession without obedience — exactly what Jeremiah confronted. Judah said, We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us, and it was true in the narrowest sense: they had the scrolls, the temple, the scribes, the machinery. And they did not know the judgment of the LORD. The modern parallel is not hard to find. Shelves of study Bibles, sermons in every pocket, commentary without end, and a generation that cannot tell the season it is in or repent when the hour has come. Access to the Word has never been greater and the stork’s rebuke has never been sharper: the bird kept its appointment, and the men with the library missed theirs.

The doctrine to recover is the twofold witness of creation. First, it convicts: the ox knows his owner and the ass his master’s crib, but Israel doth not know (Isa 1:3), and the stork’s punctual wings leave the disobedient without excuse. Second, it comforts: the same God who fixed the stork’s appointed times and gave her the fir trees for a house governs every season of His people’s lives, and not one of their appointed times is left to chance. But the bird obeys by instinct, and no instinct will ever make a rebel obedient. What creation can only expose, the Spirit must cure — and He does, writing the law upon the heart of a people who once knew the judgment of the LORD no better than Judah did.
roots_summary: The “kind one” — a migratory bird whose unfailing seasons rebuke covenant people who miss theirs.
roots_lines: Stork — Old English storc; Hebrew chasidah, from chesed, “kindness.”
Named for the kindness it shows in caring for its young.
Unclean for the table, yet honoured as a witness (Lev 11:19).
The fir trees are her house, by the Creator’s provision (Psa 104:17).
She knows her appointed times; my people know not the judgment of the LORD (Jer 8:7).
usage: The stork keeps her appointed times; the covenant people missed theirs.
A bird without a Bible obeyed; a nation with the scrolls did not.
Creation’s instinct leaves men without excuse, but only the Spirit makes a rebel obedient.

etymology: From the Old English ra, a roe, joined to buck, the male of the deer; hence the male roe-deer, rendering the Hebrew tsebi, a small swift gazelle-like deer.
biblical_def: The roebuck is the male of the roe, a small and swift deer, and it stands second in the list of beasts Israel might freely eat: “The hart, and the roebuck, and the fallow deer, and the wild goat, and the pygarg, and the wild ox, and the chamois” (Deu 14:5). Unlike the sacrificial animals, it was not an offering beast — a wild creature taken in the field, clean because it parted the hoof and chewed the cud, and eaten in ordinary houses without ceremony. That is the force of Moses’ grant of common meat: “the unclean and the clean may eat thereof, as of the roebuck, and as of the hart” (Deu 12:15). Here is the goodness of God in the daily table, a mercy easily missed under the shadow of the altar. Yet the roe’s chief service in Scripture is as a figure of swiftness. Solomon urges the man snared in a rash suretyship, “Deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter, and as a bird from the hand of the fowler” (Pro 6:5) — get out, and do not stroll out. And the Song lifts the figure higher still: “My beloved is like a roe or a young hart: behold, he standeth behind our wall” (Son 2:9). Christ comes to His bride with the roe’s swiftness — leaping the mountains, not delaying, hastening toward His people.
webster_summary: The male of the roe, a small swift deer; a clean beast of Israel’s table and a figure of swiftness.
webster_full: ROEBUCK, the male of the roe, a species of deer of small size and remarkable swiftness.
From Old English ra, a roe, and buck, the male of the deer.
Renders the Hebrew tsebi, a gazelle-like deer of the open country.
Named second among the clean beasts of Deu 14:5.
Eaten as common meat in the gates, not offered on the altar (Deu 12:15).
scriptures: Deu 14:5
The hart, and the roebuck, and the fallow deer, and the wild goat, and the pygarg, and the wild ox, and the chamois.

Notwithstanding thou mayest kill and eat flesh in all thy gates, whatsoever thy soul lusteth after, according to the blessing of the LORD thy God which he hath given thee: the unclean and the clean may eat thereof, as of the roebuck, and as of the hart.
Pro 6:5
Deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter, and as a bird from the hand of the fowler.
Son 2:9
My beloved is like a roe or a young hart: behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, shewing himself through the lattice.
corruption_summary: The Song’s roe is flattened into mere human romance; Scripture’s own use makes the Beloved’s swiftness a picture of Christ hastening to His church.
corruption_paragraphs: The live misreading concerns Son 2:9. A generation trained to read the Song only as married love has lost half of it. The Song is indeed a true celebration of covenanted love between one man and one woman, and the dictionary holds that plain sense without embarrassment. But the whole line of the Reformers and the Puritans — and before them the prophets, who make the LORD the Husband of His people — read the Beloved leaping upon the mountains as Christ coming to His church. To strip that off in the name of a sober literalism is not sobriety; it is loss. Scripture itself marries the two: the one-flesh union is a great mystery, and Paul says he speaks concerning Christ and the church.

The doctrine to hold is the swiftness of Christ toward His own. The roe is the emblem of speed, and the picture is not of a Saviour reluctantly persuaded but of one who comes leaping, skipping the hills, standing already behind the wall and looking through the lattice while the bride still thinks Him far off. Sinners imagine God must be coaxed. The Song says He is nearer than they think and moving faster than they hoped. The same swiftness that Solomon commends to the man escaping a snare — deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter — is the swiftness with which the Beloved crosses the mountains to reach her.
roots_summary: The male roe-deer — a clean beast of the common table and the Scriptural emblem of swiftness.
roots_lines: Roebuck — Old English ra + buck; Hebrew tsebi.
A small deer of great speed, taken in the field rather than the fold.
Second in the list of clean beasts (Deu 14:5).
Eaten as ordinary meat in the gates, never offered on the altar (Deu 12:15).
The emblem of swiftness in flight (Pro 6:5) and of the Beloved’s haste (Son 2:9).
usage: Clean, but not a sacrifice: the roebuck fed Israel’s table, not the altar.
Deliver thyself as a roe: escape the snare swiftly, and do not stroll out of it.
My beloved is like a roe — Christ comes to His church at speed.

etymology: From the French chamois, a goat-antelope of the high Alps, through Late Latin camox; used in the Authorized Version for the Hebrew zemer, a wild leaping creature of the mountains.
biblical_def: The chamois is a goat-antelope of the high crags, sure-footed on ledges where no other beast will stand. The Authorized translators used the name for the Hebrew zemer, and it closes the roll of clean beasts: “The hart, and the roebuck, and the fallow deer, and the wild goat, and the pygarg, and the wild ox, and the chamois” (Deu 14:5). Every creature on that list is a wild beast of field and mountain, not a herd animal of the fold, and all of them qualify by the same rule: “every beast that parteth the hoof, and cleaveth the cleft into two claws, and cheweth the cud among the beasts, that ye shall eat” (Deu 14:6). The mark of cleanness was not tameness. God did not restrict His people to what they could pen; He opened the mountain to them. Which animal the Hebrew zemer names is not certain to us — the wild sheep and the mountain gazelle are both proposed — and that uncertainty is a limit of our knowledge of the beasts of ancient Canaan, not a defect in the Word that named it. Moses named a creature his hearers knew on sight. And the closing purpose of the whole ordinance stands unshaken: the law was given “to make a difference between the unclean and the clean” (Lev 11:47), a difference God draws and man receives.
webster_summary: A goat-antelope of the high mountains; the last named of the clean beasts of Deu 14:5.
webster_full: CHAMOIS, a species of goat-antelope inhabiting the highest mountains, of remarkable agility.
From the French chamois, Late Latin camox.
Used in the Authorized Version for the Hebrew zemer, a wild leaping beast.
The last named in the list of clean beasts (Deu 14:5).
Clean by the twofold rule — parting the hoof and chewing the cud (Deu 14:6).
scriptures: Deu 14:5
The hart, and the roebuck, and the fallow deer, and the wild goat, and the pygarg, and the wild ox, and the chamois.
Deu 14:6
And every beast that parteth the hoof, and cleaveth the cleft into two claws, and cheweth the cud among the beasts, that ye shall eat.
To make a difference between the unclean and the clean, and between the beast that may be eaten and the beast that may not be eaten.
For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving:
corruption_summary: The clean-beast list is read as ancient taboo; it is in fact a charter of liberty, and its principle survives in the thanksgiving of 1Ti 4:4.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is asceticism — the persistent religious instinct that holiness is measured by what a man refuses. It was already at work in Paul’s day among teachers “commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving,” and it has never gone out of fashion, only changed its vocabulary. The list in Deu 14:5 cuts against it. Seven wild beasts are named, the mountain is opened, and the whole grant is framed as blessing rather than restriction. God gave Israel a boundary and inside that boundary He gave them abundance. Where men make their own boundaries and call the narrowing holiness, they have exchanged a father’s table for a taskmaster’s.

The principle to recover is that cleanness is God’s to define and gratitude is man’s to render. The law drew the line — parted hoof, chewed cud — and Israel did not vote on it. The gospel has not made the line looser; it has moved it off the plate entirely, for “every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:4). Note the condition. Liberty is not licence to eat thanklessly; the creature is sanctified by the word of God and prayer. The chamois on its ledge and the meal on a Christian’s table both come from the same open hand, and both are received rightly only when the hand is acknowledged.
roots_summary: A goat-antelope of the crags — the last of the seven clean beasts named to Israel.
roots_lines: Chamois — French chamois, Late Latin camox; Hebrew zemer.
A sure-footed mountain beast, agile on ledges no herd animal will cross.
The seventh and last of the clean beasts of Deu 14:5.
Clean by parting the hoof and chewing the cud (Deu 14:6).
Its exact species is uncertain to us, though it was plain to Moses’ hearers.
usage: The clean list is full of wild beasts: God opened the mountain, not merely the fold.
Cleanness was never tameness — it was the mark God set, and man received.
Every creature of God is good, received with thanksgiving — and not otherwise.

etymology: English wild with ass, from the Latin asinus; rendering the Hebrew pere' and 'arod, the untamed onager of the desert, proverbial for a freedom no man can bridle.
biblical_def: The wild ass is the onager of the wilderness — the untamed cousin of the patient beast of burden, ranging the barren places, scorning the driver, mocked at by no bridle. In Job, God Himself loosed its bands and gave it the wilderness for a house; the creature no man can break is kept by the LORD. Scripture then turns the picture upon man. Of Ishmael it is said, “he will be a wild man; his hand will be against every man, and every man’s hand against him” (Gen 16:12). Of Israel in her idolatry, “A wild ass used to the wilderness, that snuffeth up the wind at her pleasure; in her occasion who can turn her away?” (Jer 2:24). Of Ephraim running to Assyria, “a wild ass alone by himself” (Hos 8:9). And of every son of Adam by nature, “vain man would be wise, though man be born like a wild ass’s colt” (Job 11:12). This is the doctrine of the will. The natural man calls his ungoverned course freedom, and it is nothing of the kind: he snuffs up the wind at his pleasure and cannot be turned, because “the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be” (Rom 8:7). He is not free; he is a beast in a desert, doing exactly what his nature requires. And the desert does not feed him: “the wild asses did stand in the high places, they snuffed up the wind like dragons; their eyes did fail, because there was no grass” (Jer 14:6). Only the Son makes free indeed.
webster_summary: The untamed onager of the desert; the standing biblical figure of the natural man’s ungoverned will.
webster_full: WILD ASS, the onager, an untamed animal of the ass kind inhabiting the deserts of the east.
From wild and ass, Latin asinus; Hebrew pere' and 'arod.
It ranges the barren places, refusing the bridle and the driver’s cry.
Applied to Ishmael, to apostate Judah, and to Ephraim (Gen 16:12; Jer 2:24; Hos 8:9).
Man is said to be born like a wild ass’s colt (Job 11:12).
scriptures: And he will be a wild man; his hand will be against every man, and every man's hand against him; and he shall dwell in the presence of all his brethren.
Jer 14:6
And the wild asses did stand in the high places, they snuffed up the wind like dragons; their eyes did fail, because there was no grass.
Hos 8:9
For they are gone up to Assyria, a wild ass alone by himself: Ephraim hath hired lovers.
For vain man would be wise, though man be born like a wild ass's colt.
corruption_summary: Autonomy is preached as freedom; Scripture calls the ungoverned will a wilderness beast and reserves the word free for the man the Son has loosed.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the age’s central creed: that liberty means the absence of any authority above the self. Be true to yourself, follow your heart, let no man bridle you — it is the wild ass’s gospel, and Jeremiah wrote its epitaph long before it was fashionable. He watched Judah snuff up the wind at her pleasure and asked the question the modern man never asks: in her occasion who can turn her away? Not a compliment. A diagnosis. The creature that cannot be turned is not sovereign; it is enslaved to its own appetite, running a course fixed by a nature it did not choose. What our culture markets as self-determination, the prophets classify as a beast’s instinct dressed in a man’s clothes.

The doctrine to recover is the bondage of the will and the freedom Christ gives. Fallen man’s will is not neutral, poised between good and evil and waiting to be persuaded; it is bound, because the carnal mind is enmity against God and cannot be subject to His law (Rom 8:7). He sins freely in the sense that he does what he wants, and he is bound absolutely in that he cannot want otherwise until he is made new. That is why the gospel is not advice to the wild ass but a new nature for it. “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free” (Gal 5:1); “If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed” (Joh 8:36). The ranging beast of the desert is broken to the yoke of Christ, and finds for the first time that the yoke is easy and the wilderness was the prison.
roots_summary: The onager — the desert ass no man bridles, and Scripture’s figure of the unregenerate will.
roots_lines: Wild ass — Hebrew pere' and 'arod, the onager of the eastern deserts.
God loosed its bands and gave it the wilderness for a house (Job 39).
Ishmael is a wild man, his hand against every man (Gen 16:12).
Apostate Judah snuffeth up the wind at her pleasure (Jer 2:24).
Man is born like a wild ass’s colt (Job 11:12).
usage: A wild ass used to the wilderness: the ungoverned will, mistaken for liberty.
In her occasion who can turn her away? — that is a diagnosis, not a compliment.
The natural man does what he wants and cannot want otherwise until he is made new.
